props.title: Amongst White Clouds

sections.content: **Amongst White Clouds** (2005) stands as a remarkable entry in contemplative documentary filmmaking, following American director Edward Burger as he immerses himself with Buddhist hermits in China's Zhongnan Mountains. The film shares DNA with Werner Herzog's **Wheel of Time** (2003) and Philip Gröning's **Into Great Silence** (2005), but strips away even more artifice. Unlike the institutional Buddhism shown in most Western documentaries, Burger captures the raw, lived experience of monks who've rejected modern life entirely. The film's patient, observational style echoes its subjects' mindset.

movies.title: Why Has Bodhi-Dharma Left for the East?
movies.slug: A meditative Korean film following three generations of Buddhist monks living in a remote mountain monastery.

sections.content: The visual approach of **Amongst White Clouds** connects to a broader tradition of "mountain films" that explore spiritual seeking in high places. From Frank Capra's **Lost Horizon** (1937) to Michael Powell's **Black Narcissus** (1947), Western cinema has long associated mountain monasteries with enlightenment. But Burger's documentary strips away the exoticism, showing instead the mundane reality of chopping wood, gathering water, and maintaining simple meditation practices.

The film's influence can be seen in later works like **Walking the Mountain** (2009) and **Paths of the Soul** (2015), which similarly document Buddhist practices in remote Chinese locations. However, **Amongst White Clouds** remains unique in its intimate access to true hermits, many of whom had never been filmed before and likely never will be again. The authenticity of these encounters provides a rare window into a vanishing way of life. SUBHEAD: The Hermit Tradition in Cinema

movies.title: Zen for Nothing
movies.slug: A Swiss woman's journey into a Japanese Zen monastery, offering an outsider's perspective on monastic life.

sections.content: While most Buddhist-themed films focus on monasteries or teachers, the hermit tradition has its own distinct cinematic lineage. **Cave of Silence** (1995) explored Japanese mountain ascetics, while **Himalaya** (1999) touched on Tibetan hermits. **Amongst White Clouds** stands out by focusing exclusively on individual practitioners who have rejected even monastery life, showing how true solitude shapes their practice and understanding.
